sections.history: Thiruchenkundrur, today better known as the Thrichittatt Maha Vishnu Temple, lies about two kilometres north-west of Chengannur in Alappuzha district. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Malai Nadu, the Kerala country. Its presiding lord is Imayavarappan, who stands in the sanctum with Sengamalavalli Thayar as his consort. Nammalvar sang of the shrine in his Thiruvaimozhi. Inscriptions are said to place the structure somewhere between the eighth and twelfth centuries CE, and the temple is administered today by the Travancore Devaswom Board. Tradition counts it among the five Vishnu temples of the Chengannur country, each attributed to one of the Pandava brothers; this one is Yudhishthira’s.
sections.architecture: The sanctum is crowned by the Jagajjyoti vimana, and the temple’s sacred tank, the Sankha Theertham, lies to the right beyond the entrance arch. Within, Imayavarappan is worshipped standing, while the Goddess Sengamalavalli is honoured as his consort. The precinct is ordered in the manner of the Kerala temple, calm and inward-looking, with the tank and the sanctum as its two quiet centres of devotion.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that Yudhishthira, eldest of the Pandavas, did penance at this place for the half-truth about “Ashwatthama” that brought down his teacher Drona. The shrine is one of five around Chengannur that are each attributed to a Pandava: Thrichittatt to Yudhishthira, Puliyur to Bhima, Aranmula to Arjuna, Thiruvanvandoor to Nakula and Thrikodithanam to Sahadeva. Together they are remembered as the Pancha Pandava temples. The name Thrichittatt itself is traditionally linked with the river Chitraru.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps an annual utsavam in the manner of Kerala’s Vishnu temples, and observes Vaikunta Ekadashi, the most sacred day of the Vaishnava year, when devotees come in larger numbers. Exact festival dates follow the temple’s own calendar, so ask locally or check with the Devaswom office before planning a visit around them.
sections.experience: A quiet pilgrimage stop close to Chengannur, best combined with the other four Pandava-linked Vishnu temples of the area. Walk first to the Sankha Theertham, then enter for darshan of the standing Imayavarappan. Devotees who know Nammalvar’s Thiruvaimozhi may like to recall its verses here, in the very country the Alvar sang of.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions, usually with a midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 2 km north-west of Chengannur town in Alappuzha district; Chengannur railway station is the nearest, with autorickshaws and taxis for the short ride. Chengannur is linked by road to Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Alappuzha; Thiruvananthapuram and Kochi are the usual airport gateways.
